Conversation notebook / English

July 2–11, 2026 · 10 sessions

Three small patterns to carry into conversation.

Focus on the form just after suggest and interested in, then check the verb when telling a finished past story.

The first two patterns recur across sessions. The past-tense examples are clustered in one session. These notes describe the recorded examples—not how often you make errors overall.

01Passing on a suggestionUse “suggested that I…” 02Talking about interestsUse “interested in learning” 03Telling a past storyMatch the verb to the time

Not every suggested change is a correction. Several of your original sentences were already natural. Keep those choices; there is no need to make casual conversation more formal. See what to keep.

1

Suggest an action—not “someone to do”

Recurring across sessions · 4 records in 4 sessions

From your record · original

She suggested me to take a break.

Recommended correction

She suggested that I take a break.

Source trail · 4 sessions

The same original sentence and correction appear in all four records. They support a repeated sentence pattern, not four different types of error.

N01-U03 · N04-U03 · N07-U03 · N10-U03

A useful frame to remember

When you name the person who should act, use suggest + that + person + verb.

She suggested that I take a break.

Use take here, without to. The past form suggested tells us when the suggestion happened.

Another option: “She suggested taking a break.” This focuses on the action without explicitly naming who should take the break.

Try it in a different conversation · optional

New learning example · not from your history

A colleague gave us an idea. Complete the sentence:
“He suggested ___ before the meeting.”

Make it yours, if you like: think of advice someone gave you. Start with “They suggested that I…”

2

After “interested in,” use an -ing action

Recurring across sessions · 3 records in 3 sessions

From your record · original

I am interested in learn more about plants.

Recommended correction

I am interested in learning more about plants.

Source trail · 3 sessions

The same sentence appears in each of these records. The actionable change is from “learn” to “learning” after the preposition “in.”

N02-U03 · N05-U03 · N08-U03

Keep “in” attached to what follows

You can be interested in a thing, such as plants. When you name an action after in, use its -ing form.

interested in + learning / trying / visiting

A helpful connection: your sentence “I am looking forward to seeing you” already uses this kind of structure correctly. In “look forward to,” to is a preposition, so keep seeing.

Source trail · the correct connection

Original in both records: “I am looking forward to seeing you.” The proposed change to “see” should not be used.

N04-U01 · N10-U01

Choose the next word · optional

New learning example · not from your history

You want to try a new hobby:
“I'm interested in ___ a pottery class.”

Make it yours, if you like: “I'm interested in…” + an activity you might try.

3

Let the time cue change the verb

Clustered in one session · 3 records, all from July 7

From your record: original → recommended correction

Yesterday I go to the market.

Yesterday I went to the market.

Last Friday I buy a used bicycle.

Last Friday I bought a used bicycle.

I see that film last night.

I saw that film last night.

Source trail · 1 session

The notes describe all three events as completed in the past. This supports a useful past-tense check, but does not establish recurrence across sessions.

Market: N06-U03
Bicycle: N06-U04
Film: N06-U05

“Yesterday” is a cue—not a substitute

For a completed event, the time expression and the verb work together. Even with yesterday or last night, use the past form in these statements.

go → went   ·   buy → bought   ·   see → saw

Before telling a past story, bring its main verb to mind: “Yesterday… went.” These three verbs have irregular past forms; adding -ed won't work.

Tell a tiny past story · optional

New learning example · not from your history

Choose the pair for a completed trip:
“Last Saturday I ___ to the bookshop and ___ a novel.”

Make it yours, if you like: say one sentence about yesterday using went, bought, or saw.

Keep your natural English

These originals do not need fixing.

The context matters. Open any sentence to see why the proposed change is unnecessary—or would change your meaning.

“I have a little time this evening.”

You meant that you had some time available. “A little time” expresses that. “Little time,” without a, suggests almost none, so it would change your message.

Original sentence · N03-U01 · N09-U01

“I am looking forward to seeing you.”

This is correct as written. In this expression, to is a preposition: use seeing, not “see.”

Original sentence · N04-U01 · N10-U01

“Because I was tired.”

The recorded context was an answer to “Why did you stop?” In that exchange, this short answer is natural and complete enough. “I stopped because I was tired” is an optional expansion.

Original answer and recorded context · N02-U01 · N08-U01

“I bought a coffee before the train.”

You ordered one cup. A coffee is normal when referring to one serving; you do not need to remove the article.

Original sentence · N06-U01

“I think the plan is pretty good.”

This is grammatical, natural casual English. “I believe the plan is quite good” is an optional change in wording and tone, not a necessary correction.

Original sentence · N01-U01 · N07-U01

“The person who I spoke to was friendly.”

This is ordinary conversational English. “The person to whom I spoke…” is more formal; it is not required in casual conversation.
